info.title: How much should you eat for balanced nutrition?

sections.heading: Daily energy needs
items: Energy need = Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) × activity factor: sedentary ×1.2, light activity (1-3 sessions/week) ×1.375, moderate (3-5 sessions/week) ×1.55, heavy (6-7 sessions/week) ×1.725.
General estimate for adults: roughly 1,800–2,200 kcal/day for women, 2,200–2,800 kcal/day for men, depending on actual activity level.

sections.heading: 4 food groups every meal needs
items: Carbs: rice, noodles, potatoes, whole grains.
Protein: meat, fish, eggs, beans, dairy.
Vegetables & fruit: vitamins, minerals, and fiber.
Healthy fats: vegetable oils, fatty fish (salmon, mackerel), nuts.

sections.heading: Good meal timing
items: Eat 3 regular meals at consistent times — don't skip breakfast.
Finish dinner at least 2-3 hours before bedtime to give digestion time to wind down.

sources.label: National Institute of Nutrition Vietnam — Recommended Dietary Allowances

info.title: When is the best time to exercise?

sections.heading: Activity guidelines (WHO 2020)
items: Adults: 150–300 minutes/week of moderate activity, or 75–150 minutes of vigorous activity, or an equivalent combination.
Add muscle-strengthening exercises (weights, push-ups, squats...) for all major muscle groups, at least 2 days/week.
Going beyond the minimum (up to 300-750 minutes/week moderate) provides additional health benefits.

sections.heading: Best time to train
items: Early morning (1-2 hours after waking): helps you stay alert and focused all day.
Late afternoon (4-7 PM): body temperature and muscle strength peak — good for heavier training.
Avoid vigorous training close to bedtime (within 1-2 hours) as it can make it harder to fall asleep.

sections.heading: Recovery
items: Aim for at least 1-2 rest days per week so muscles and joints can recover and reduce injury risk.

sources.label: WHO — Guidelines on Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour (2020)
CDC — Physical Activity Basics for Adults

water.title: Have you drunk enough water today?
water.subtitle: Cast your vote below. Each device can vote once per day.

sections.heading: Daily recommended intake
items: National Academies of Sciences (NASEM): adult women average ~2.7 liters/day total water (including food), men ~3.7 liters/day — roughly 8-13 cups of 250ml as direct drinking water depending on the person.
Children 4–8 years old: about 1.2 liters/day; teens 9–18: about 1.6–1.9 liters/day.

sections.heading: How to drink it right
items: Spread it out — 150–250ml per serving, roughly every 1-2 hours. Don't wait until you're thirsty.
Drink more during intense exercise, hot weather, or when sick with fever/diarrhea.

sections.heading: Signs you're dehydrated
items: Thirst, dry mouth, dark and reduced urine output.
Fatigue, headache, dizziness, trouble concentrating.
Muscle cramps from electrolyte imbalance.

sources.label: National Academies of Sciences — Dietary Reference Intakes for Water
Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health — The Nutrition Source: Water

sleep.title: Did you get enough sleep last night?
sleep.subtitle: Cast your vote below. Each device can vote once per day.

sections.heading: Recommended hours by age
items: Adults (18-64): 7-9 hours/night.
Older adults (65+): 7-8 hours/night.
Teens (14-17): 8-10 hours/night.
School-age children (6-13): 9-11 hours/night.

sections.heading: Good sleep hygiene
items: Go to bed and wake up at consistent times every day, weekends included.
Keep your bedroom dark, quiet and cool to fall asleep more easily.
Avoid phone/computer screens for at least 30-60 minutes before bed.
Limit caffeine, alcohol, and large amounts of fluid close to bedtime.
If you nap, keep it to 15-30 minutes so it doesn't disrupt nighttime sleep.

sections.heading: Consequences of chronic sleep debt
items: Reduced focus and memory, higher risk of cardiovascular disease, obesity, and mood disorders.

sources.label: National Sleep Foundation — Sleep Duration Recommendations
